chapter.title: Pick one destination

cards.body: Imagine leading five friends on a walk through a town none of them know. Before anyone laces a shoe, you say: **we're going to the lighthouse.** Not 'the lighthouse, and maybe the harbour, and there's a nice bakery': one place, named out loud, so everyone knows what arriving looks like.
cards.simpler: Picture yourself taking five friends on a walk through a town none of you know. Before anyone puts their shoes on, you tell them: **we're going to the lighthouse.** Not the lighthouse, plus maybe the harbour, plus a nice bakery. Just one place, said out loud. Now everyone knows what it looks like to arrive.

cards.prompt: Dev is giving a 3-minute talk to his running club. He says it's about 'training, nutrition, sleep, and why I started running'. In walk terms, where is he taking them?

options.text: To the lighthouse, by a scenic route.
To four places at once, which is nowhere.
To the lighthouse, with a quick stop at the bakery.

whyNot.a: That's a route with one destination, not Dev's list: he named four topics and no single place to arrive.
whyNot.c: That's one destination plus a detour: Dev has no main destination at all, just four equal stops.

cards.reteach: A destination is one place everyone can picture arriving at. Dev's four topics are four separate walks. Until he picks one, nobody, including Dev, knows when the talk is finished.

cards.title: A point, not a topic
cards.body:
A *topic* is an area, like 'running'. A *point* is one thing you want listeners to believe or do when you stop, like 'run slower than you think you should'. **A talk needs a point, not a topic.** A topic has no end. A point does.

Here's the test. A friend asks 'what's your talk about?' If you can answer in one sentence that starts with 'that', you have a point. 'That running slower builds speed' passes. 'Running' fails.

Everything else in the talk, every story and number, exists to carry people to that one sentence.
cards.simpler:
A topic is a subject, like 'running'. A point is one thing you want people to believe or do by the end, like 'run slower than you think'. **A talk needs a point, not a topic.**

Test it. A friend asks what your talk is about. If you can answer in one sentence starting with 'that', you have a point. 'That running slower builds speed' works. 'Running' fails. Every story and number carries people to that sentence.

cards.title: Priya's 13 words
cards.body:
Priya had to give a 3-minute talk at work about a new expenses app. Her first draft point was 'the new expenses system'. That's a topic. Nobody can arrive at a system.

Her second try: 'Submit receipts the same day you spend, because the app does the rest.' 13 words. Her colleague Tom read it and said 'oh, so I just photograph the receipt at lunch?' That's what arriving sounds like: **someone repeats your point back in their own words.**
cards.simpler:
Priya had to give a 3-minute talk at work about a new expenses app. Her first point was 'the new expenses system'. That's a topic. Nobody can arrive at a system.

Her second try: 'Submit receipts the same day you spend, because the app does the rest.' 13 words. Her colleague Tom read it and said, 'oh, so I just photograph the receipt at lunch?' That's what arriving sounds like: **someone repeats your point back in their own words.**

cards.prompt: Which of these is a destination, written the way this chapter asks?

options.text: Why our team should switch to a four-day week.
Give the team Fridays off and output goes up, because tired people make mistakes.
The four-day week: history, evidence, and what it would mean for us.

whyNot.a: That's a title, not a point: it names the area but doesn't say what you want people to believe at the end.
whyNot.c: That's an agenda, not a point: three stops and no single place to arrive.

cards.reteach: The destination is a full sentence someone could agree or disagree with. 'Why we should switch' is a question you haven't answered yet. 'Give Fridays off and output goes up' is the answer, said plainly, and that's what the talk delivers.

cards.title: Write it first, in 15 words
cards.body:
Write the sentence **before you write anything else.** Not the opening, not the slides, not the story you're excited to tell. If you write the talk first and hunt for the point afterwards, you'll find three, and you'll keep all of them.

Keep it to 15 words or fewer. That limit is a tool, not a style choice. At 15 words there's no room for a second idea to hide behind an 'and'.

Then say it out loud. If it takes more than 10 seconds, or you stumble halfway, it's two sentences wearing one coat.
cards.simpler:
Write the sentence **before you write anything else.** Not the opening, not the slides, not your favourite story. Write the talk first and hunt for the point later, and you'll find three and keep them all.

Keep it to 15 words or fewer. The limit is a tool. At 15 words, a second idea has nowhere to hide behind an 'and'.

Say it out loud. If it takes over 10 seconds, or you stumble, it's two sentences in one coat.

cards.body: Marcus wrote his point: 'Our onboarding takes too long and new hires feel lost and we should fix the handbook.' 17 words, two 'and's. He was proud of it. His talk ran 6 minutes and ended three times. Spot it in your own sentence: **count the 'and's.** Each one is probably a second destination you haven't let go of yet.
cards.simpler: Marcus wrote his point: 'Our onboarding takes too long and new hires feel lost and we should fix the handbook.' 17 words, two 'and's. He was proud of it. His talk ran 6 minutes and ended three times. Check your own sentence the same way: **count the 'and's.** Each one is probably a second destination you haven't let go of yet.

cards.prompt: You've got a 3-minute talk tomorrow. What's the first thing you write?

options.text: A strong opening line to hook the room.
The one sentence you want people to leave believing, in 15 words or fewer.
A list of the 3 or 4 topics you'll cover.

whyNot.a: That's the first step of the walk, not the destination: you can't plan an opening until you know where it's heading. Chapter 4 covers it.
whyNot.c: That's a list of topics, not a point: four topics is four walks, and nobody arrives anywhere.

cards.reteach: Everything in a talk is chosen by one question: does this move people toward the point? You can't ask that question until the point exists. So the sentence comes first, and the opening, stories and lists come after.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A talk is a walk to one place, so before you write anything else, write the one sentence you want people to leave believing, in 15 words or fewer. **If it has an 'and' in it, it's probably two talks.**
cards.simpler: A talk is a walk to one place. So before you write anything else, write the one sentence you want people to leave believing. Keep it to 15 words or fewer. **If it has an 'and' in it, it's probably two talks.**

cards.body: Open your notes app. Type the one sentence for any talk, toast or meeting update you have coming up. Under 15 words. Read it aloud once and time it: under 10 seconds.
cards.simpler: Open the notes app on your phone or computer. Type the one sentence for any talk, toast or meeting update you have coming up. **Keep it under 15 words.** Then read it out loud once and time yourself. It should take under 10 seconds.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write the one sentence your talk exists to deliver, and say it out loud in under 10 seconds.
